utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radinkovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Radinkovic, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that might suggest you have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Radinkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for making a pause between questions and answers, and you should remind me, too, to make a sufficiently long pause for everything to be recorded. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown in e-court 1D49035.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the front page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in full.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness the last page to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you have said to the Defence team? Is there anything you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: All of it is exactly what I said, what I was able to remember after all this time, and at this time I have no additions to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today as those put to you by my associates, would your answers be essentially the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: They believed be completely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them both. Shall we assign the numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement received Exhibit Number D4204. The associated exhibit 05460 receives Exhibit Number D4205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read in English the summary of Mr. Radomir Radinkovic's statement. [In English] Radomir Radinkovic was mobilised on June the 21st, 1991, and served as an OB (intelligence and security) officer in the JNA. He was mobilised into the VRS in May 1992 and was also assigned to the post of intelligence and security officer at the 1st Krajina Corps. The Manjaca camp was set up by the command of the JNA and it served as a camp for the prisoners of war captured in Stara Gradiska in Croatia. The police were in charge of external security and the military police were in charge of the internal security. Civilian police only went inside the camp when bringing in new prisoners, while military police went into the camp compound to bring people in for questioning or for medical examinations. No one ever ordered or allowed that the rights of prisoners be violated and every effort was made to protect the prisoners from irresponsible individuals. It will role of the OB was to ensure security and safety in the camp, to report to the superior command, and to propose protective measures. Reports were sent at least once week, and sometimes on a daily basis and addressed all the issues of importance for the security. The civilian police interrogated prisoners in the camp in order to examine them and to document any previously committed crimes. They did this with the knowledge and approval of the OB chief of the 1st Krajina Corps. Upon their arrival, prisoners were made aware of their rights and obligations in connection with the status of prisoners of war and their state in the camp. Medical examinations were then performed, and hygiene and prevention measures were taken before transferring prisoners to their assigned accommodation in the facility. All those who worked on breaking up the state were considered and treated as the extremists. Security services submitted information about the individuals who had taken part in incidents in the field so that measures could be taken to prevent other security incidents. Specifically, they had intelligence about the extreme activities of Omer Filipovic, who was the founder of the SDA in Kljuc and who established a paramilitary formation in the area. Most prisoners in the Manjaca camp were Muslims, some were Croats, and there were a few Serbs. Prisoners were selected and released based on the evaluation and proposals by the operational team of the OB, by the camp commander, medical services, and the approval of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. The killing of Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender have been done by some members of the military police acting on their own volition. This case was dealt by the crime-fighting service of the military police battalion. The perpetrators were suspended and criminal proceedings were instigated against them. After the war, they were convicted by the district court in Banja Luka. Prisoners of war were given status under the Geneva Conventions, which meant that they were registered and verified, that lists were compiled, health care was provided, together with the regular meals, sufficient quantities of drinking water, and accommodation, and that they were allowed visits by the ICRC through whom they maintained contact with their families. People caught without weapons could also be considered as prisoners of war, in case they assisted members of the armed forces or put up unarmed resistance. The ICRC reports on the treatment of the prisoners are generally accurate; however, sections of these reports are biased. They failed to take into account the general situation and the inability to ensure better conditions. Some people were held in the camps for their own safety. The ICRC and many journalists were granted approval to visit the camp by President Karadzic. Some of the prisoners were released on 14th of November, 1992. This group was composed by the young, the elderly, and those in extremely poor health. Some sick prisoners were also pardoned and sent to Geneva for medical treatment. No more prisoners were transferred to the Manjaca camp after 6th of August, 1992, and in December 1992 the camp was closed. If someone from security harassed prisoners of war, measures were taken against them. Charges were brought against the perpetrators responsible for incidents in the camp and most of them have already been processed. Within the possibilities at the time, maximum treatment was provided in terms of accommodation, water supply, food, medical treatment, and hygiene. Vojo Kupresanin, a leading man in the ARK, visited the camp in 1992. The aim of his visit was to convince the prisoners of war that a solution would be found as to the question of their release from custody. He also issued a document pardoning some prisoners of war. The Republika Srpska leadership did not order or recommend the ill-treatment or liquidation of prisoners of war. And that is the summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radinkovic, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement. Now, you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radinkovic, I'd like to start your cross-examination by getting you to confirm some information about Manjaca that's additional to what you spoke about in your statement. First, you can confirm, I take it, that particularly between June and August 1992 Manjaca received a massive number of prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and even the number of these arrivals is stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well -- okay, talking about the number, at its -- its fullest, the prisoner population at Manjaca was in excess of 3.500 people; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: It never reached that number at any one time. The maximum at one time was around 2.000, because some people left and new ones came. They departed to be exchanged. They were transported to third countries or elsewhere. And some new people came.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now, are you quite sure about those figures? Because I've read your testimony that you gave in 2011 to the state court in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there you said that the population ranged, actually. At page 29, you said it was almost 3.000, and then at page 68 you said at one point it went up to maybe 4-, 4.500?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said. It varied. Sometimes there were more, sometimes less. That's what I was trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. And you talked in your written evidence about the ethnic background of the prisoners at Manjaca, and in the summary of your evidence Dr. Karadzic said that most were Bosnian Muslims. In fact, over 85 per cent were Bosniaks; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this massive amount of prisoners came predominantly to your camp from detention sites in Kljuc, Prijedor, and Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they also came from Doboj, Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: From Doboj, yes, but we have no records that anyone came from Mrkonjic Grad, maybe they were from Kljuc. But there was one group from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Jajce --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: More precisely from Rudari or some place like that. We didn't have a separate list.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Jajce?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no separate list from Jajce either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no organised transports from Bosanska Dubica. There is a possibility that some people from there were brought with groups from Prijedor and others to the Manjaca camp, but not specifically from Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, the transfer of these prisoners from all these locations to Manjaca from the areas I've just listed, that involved the co-operation of the police forces, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Transports were handled exclusively by the civilian police from other collection centres, from other towns, that was the responsibility of the civilian police. They brought these people and handed them over to Manjaca camp. By entering the camp, from the moment of entering the camp, they became prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now all of these prisoners that you said 85 per cent of were Bosniaks, the rest, the other 15 per cent were Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Croats and just a few Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to talk about what Dr. Karadzic described in his summary as their assigned accommodation. You can confirm that the prisoners at Manjaca were housed in cattle sheds; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: These structures were originally cattle sheds, but they were adapted for a different use, so they were no longer cattle sheds. They were hangars prepared especially to accommodate these prisoners of war. So everything was done to prepare these structures to be used by people, not cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Each of these cattle sheds accommodated about 7- or 800 men; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the prisoners slept on the ground where the cattle used to be tied; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: If the cattle had been tied there, still it was covered by concrete later. So it was no longer a shed. It was clean, clean straw and blankets were provided in rows so that people could sleep normally in rows.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They slept on the ground; right? They slept on the floor of the cattle sheds where the cattle used to be tied; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they used to be tied. But when you looked at it at that time, nothing would tell you that it used to be a cattle shed. It was in hygienic terms prepared for housing people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll talk a little bit more about the accommodations then, given what you've just said. And I recall in your statement, you said things like at paragraph 34, healthcare was provided, the prisoners had regular meals, they had enough drinking water. So keeping that in mind and what you've just said, I wonder if we could have a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P3758. And if we could go over to page 5, I think, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, at the bottom of this page -- oh, pardon me, this is an ICRC report on the visit -- their visit to Manjaca on 16 July 1992. And their observations and experiences. Now, this report, if you go down to paragraph 3 at the bottom says: "The general living conditions with regard to food, hygiene, clothing and accommodation ... are absolutely insufficient," Mr. Radinkovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you go over to the next page in both languages, it says at the top: "Many detainees show marked weight loss and signs of anemia with severity often corresponding to the length of detention." And, Mr. Radinkovic, this Chamber has also heard evidence from prisoners who were detained at Manjaca. They have heard evidence that there was never enough food. They have heard evidence that the prisoners were at periods so hungry that men ate grass. They've heard evidence that the water that the prisoners were given was unclean, it came from a lake where guards urinated into the lake, and even prisoners were forced to do the same. There were tadpoles swimming in the water. They have heard evidence that - and this document reports that - prisoners only had the opportunity to take a shower twice a month. And they have heard evidence that not everyone had a blanket and not everyone had straw. So, Mr. Radinkovic, when you said a little while ago that "nothing would tell you that the accommodations that they were in used to be a cattle shed," actually the evidence that we've heard suggests that not only were the prisoners accommodated in the cattle facilities, they were treated like animals. And the ICRC report we've just looked at corroborates the evidence that the prisoners have given. Nothing about the conditions were adequate, were they, Mr. Radinkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with that since these were probably statements made by individuals who, for reasons of their own, said that. I claim that most prisoners of war can confirm my position; that is to say, that at that point in time the best possible was provided by the military command, not to say the top echelons of power, because at the time, people all over Republika Srpska were hungry too. There was very little food and there weren't enough resources for hygiene and whatever. But I claim with full responsibility that at that point in time, a maximum was provided to those people. People lost a lot of weight in the camp because before the ICRC arrived, another group arrived from another centre, and then there were a lot of people there who had lost a lot of weight, and then it was presented as if some prisoners had been starved and so on and so forth. If I tell you that the food was basically identical up until the moment when the Red Cross was involved -- I mean, what people ate there is what the prisoners of war ate too. So no one had the need to graze grass. This is just an arbitrary statement made by some individuals -- some individual, that is to say, that is groundless. As for the water, yes, there is a lake there, but it is a source, quite literally a spring. And in hygienic vessels, water was brought from there for all of us who lived there because we didn't have any other water at that point in the time. That is to say that this is wrong to say that somebody was swimming there or floating or whatever. Now, further away from the camp, there was this other lake. I claim with full responsibility that everybody got two blankets. One for covering themselves and the other blanket to be put on the straw. Within the camp itself, they chose their own commanders, these facilities, these buildings had commanders of their own, and then they could bring in as much straw as they wanted. So nobody could just lie on the concrete, as that statement says. So that would be what I had to say. As for the Red Cross, they always provided their opinion. Sometimes it was positive, sometimes it was negative. There are some that are very positive. So it's not that it was all that bad, all black if you will. There were some positive opinions, too. Well, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Well, we'll come back to this document in a little while. But I want to talk a little bit more about the prison population. In the summary of your evidence, Dr. Karadzic actually confirmed that included -- just to start with, included in the prison population there were some minors; right? There were kids who were detained at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not children. There were say 18 or 19 -- well, they were not of age. They -- we said that they were minors because they were not of age yet, but the authorities that arrested them probably assessed that they should be brought in. We did not receive any description as to why that happened, but that was the selection made. And as you said yourself, I mean, children, well, they cannot really constitute any kind of danger or threat, and then they could be released or they could be taken to third countries, whatever. The camp could be left. There were such cases. And then there were also some people who were so old and frail. Regardless of what the description was over there, you would see that some man would be so old that he should be allowed to leave and so on and so forth. Let me say something else in passing: It's not contained in any one of these documents. Our medical service -- actually, we didn't really have a medical service, but at least 20 or 30 people were taken from the Manjaca camp to the clinical centre in Banja Luka for medical treatment if they were exhausted, frail, sick, and so on. Some were even transported to Geneva and places like that from there, so the treatment of these persons was very humane.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 14, line 2. [In English] "Regardless of what the description of their misdeeds ..." [Interpretation] "Regardless of what the description was of what they had done," that is not contained in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the authorities who brought in prisoners brought in some people underage. They also brought in men who were elderly, as you've just said, and people who were sick; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, now were they sick when they left? But it turned out that they were sick when they were there, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have found, then, when you and your operational team were processing the prisoners who were brought in, that the authorities who had detained them also brought you a great number who were obviously either civilians or known not to have been involved in any of the actions that supposedly justified their capture. That's fair, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not correct. We in the team did not know what guided them to arrest theme people and to bring them in. Some gave some information about the movement of our units, forces, et cetera, regardless of how old they were, and then they would fall under that, that they had participated in some way in the conflicts and so on and so forth. So we were not out there on the ground to establish who was brought in on account of what, but they were certainly grounds for bringing them there. It's not that somebody was just picked up and brought there without any kind of grounds or for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show you a document that's prepared by part of your operative team.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For that, Your Honours, we need to go into private session. It's a document that was tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Radinkovic, what you found as you and your operative team continued to work over the course of the summer was that prisoners had been captured on a purely arbitrary basis. In fact, the only thing they had in common was that they weren't Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I never said that they were arrested arbitrarily. I just said that there was the possibility that there were such persons among them. I claim with full responsibility that not a single person was arrested just because he or she was not a Serb. So it was not on ethnic grounds. Why would they arrest him if he's loyal? Do not forget that a lot of people were in the armed forces of Republika Srpska, people of other religious backgrounds, Muslims and Croats, who wanted to be there and who remained loyal to the people that they lived with and their environment, so I cannot reconcile myself to that, that somebody was just brought in because they were a Muslim or a Croat or some third thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Or they were brought in if they weren't loyal. They were brought in if they didn't want to accept the authority of a Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that nobody forced anyone to accept the authority of Republika Srpska. As a matter of fact, some people left, no problem whatsoever, and they had never had any problems and they did not put up any resistance. People simply assessed that it was better for them to leave. That was their choice. So that this was some type of pressure, I would not agree with that. No way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll go on to another area. I want to talk about pardons because you talked about that in your statement. And I want to show you -- I want to start by showing you one of your own documents. It's P5472. And it's your report -- your report of activities at the camp to the 1 KK command for the dates of 18 to 20 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we can go over to page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And page 2 in your language. You see there the last paragraph of the document says that -- it indicates you received a task from Major Stupar, which was the result of a communication from the VRS Main Staff, and in accordance with that communication called a joint meeting with representatives of the CSBs in the area and in your security department. Do you see that paragraph? And --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- at that meeting Major Stupar and Vaso Skondric presented some tasks a for joint work. Who was Vaso Skondric? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Given the time aspect, I cannot remember what the function of that man was. Probably somebody from the civilian structures of these municipalities that have been listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. And we'll see that shortly. And now based on this communication from the Main Staff, you would have had a meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's go over then to P3491. And that's an excerpt from a diary of a fellow by the name of Tode Gajic, and you remember him because you talked about him in your testimony in front of the state court. He was an inspector at the Kljuc SJB. And these are his notes about that meeting. On the 20th of August, you were among the people who sat with Major Stupar, Mr. Skondric, the camp commander, Colonel Popovic, to discuss the treatment and the prominence of persons who participated in the armed conflict. And do you see just under point number 4 your name -- where your name is, that: "Introductory remarks on the Serbian Republic Presidency's position were presented by Major Stupar."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that, both.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So there is Major Stupar's position, he's presenting the position of the Presidency, which is to release people -- release innocent people, people that you have no justification for detaining, who were so sick that that would attract the attention of the media and humanitarian organisations. So that's what Mr. Gajic's notes record; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that that's there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's what you understood the Presidency's position to be; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did because Major Stupar came from a corps command with that kind of position, the command position that he must have received on the basis of an order from the Presidency or higher organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've got a list, and we'll go to that list in a minute, of 92 candidates you have to review in regard to this position. Let's -- let's go and look at a couple of names on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 5 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So on page 5 at number 11, we see, for example, Refik Salihovic, and he was arrested on the 29th of May, and he's sick with active tuberculosis. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And number 13 on the list, Muharem Mehmedovic. He was born in 1937. He was arrested on 26 June. He has gall bladder problems, diabetes, and he can't stand. Do you see that one, too?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see Refik Dedic at number 20? He's got kidney disease. Born in 1934.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 12 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now we're on the list of minors. Do you see number 11, Denis Gromlic. There's minors born in 1974 and 1975. Denis Gromlic, who was 17 at the time he was arrested, he's one of the 92 whose cases you considered.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So these were examples of --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he must have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These were examples of the types of illnesses and disabilities you picked for release from Manjaca because of the attention they could attract; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the reason. The reason was that it was obvious that this person was young and that the others have been medically treated already, and the most logical thing was for them to go somewhere outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So we looked at this document. The first page of this document sets out the position of the Presidency, and the position of the Presidency is to release innocent people who were so sick they would attract attention from media and humanitarian organisations. My question to you was: These are examples of the people who fit that criteria; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Where does it say "innocent people"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the first page, I think we saw reference that no evidence of executing or participating in the military activities. I think that term was used in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So back to my question, Mr. Radinkovic. These are examples of the people who fit that criteria; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: These are only some examples, but others are not stated. Others for who we assessed without any medical documentation, and we reached the conclusion that it would be humane to release them from the camp. That's very important to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at P3721.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a document dated 11 September 1992, and it's a 1 KK communication forwarding the contents of a telegram from the Presidency, which grants amnesty to 69 prisoners from Manjaca and Trnopolje. Now, Mr. Radinkovic, can you have a look at this list. Number 6 is the minor Denis Gromlic, number 17 is Refik Salihovic, and number 29 is Refik Dedic. Those are the three names that I identified to you that you discussed at your meeting on the 20th of August; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And that corroborates what I said, that we released people of whom we thought that they should or actually needed to leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your list that you arrived at as a result of that meeting went up the chain of command as far as the Presidency and all the way back down again, so the decision on pardon could eventually be implemented; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this pardon of 69 people out of a prison population at Manjaca alone of -- we've talked of a number of prisoners between 2.000 and 4.500, that's actually really just a token gesture, isn't it? It's a way of avoiding some undesirable publicity from the international community and to garner some credit with them, especially in light of the story about the camps that had broken earlier on in August.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you because even before that, we had released people under the same criteria, not only pursuant to this list. There were also people released who are not on this list. This is dated the 11th of September, 1992, and people were released much earlier. Some of the released were even religious ministers or hodzas, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in addition to the sick, the elderly, civilians, people who weren't participant in combat activities, you also had religious figures in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: There were a couple and they were among the first to be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting that you didn't agree with my characterisation of this as a token gesture to garner some international credit, because that's exactly what Dr. Karadzic told his people that it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can go to D456.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's a transcript -- it's so you can read it, but I'll read it to you, it's a copy of the transcript of the 20th Assembly Session of Republika Srpska, dated 15 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we can go to English page 55. And the passage I'm going to refer to is about nine lines down from the top, and B/C/S page 58. And on page 58, it's about 16 lines up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic talked about prisoners of war. And he said: "About three weeks before they started talking about camps, we submitted a 16-page pamphlet to the British parliament, to all important foreign correspondents about concentration camps for Serbs, but no one paid any attention."

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAID
utterances.text: "Disbanding Trnopolje does not mean letting up. If they want to take them abroad, let them. They want to take 69 sick people tomorrow, let them," 69, exactly the same number of people on the pardon that I just showed you, "Let them. That will give us great credit among the international public. We want to co-operate, we want to deal with humanitarian issues, and that helps us. Don't worry about that. We don't need Manjaca. If only all the Green Berets had been killed with a rifle in their hand, but once they have been captured, then we must abide by the Geneva Conventions and it's all for nothing. It would suit us if it were shut down, disbanded, shut down and sent somewhere, but not for them to return to the battle-field." So, Mr. Radinkovic, whatever humanitarian considerations you in your operative team might have had in mind, for Dr. Karadzic, these 69 people were just a token, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the opinion of Mr. Karadzic. I respect that. The president said that and that seems to be his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And meanwhile, the great number of civilians and people who your processing showed had been detained without justification remained at Manjaca as human collateral; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: By no means. They are not a collateral damage. It was their salvation. I state that with full responsibility. If they had gone anywhere from there, individually or in small groups, it is very doubtful how they would have ended up. And there they were guarded, they were visited by the International Red Cross, and they had a certain status. It's a great question if many of them had been alive today, if they had left and went elsewhere on their own. I still maintain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You gave evidence, to switch topics, in your statement that prisoners at Manjaca were beaten. That was at paragraph 12 on page 4 and at paragraph 28. That's right, isn't it? Prisoners at Manjaca were beaten?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you saw that on arriving at Manjaca, prisoners bore the marks of having been beaten.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was established and verified and even the International Red Cross confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on their arrival at Manjaca, prisoners were also beaten. Policemen would make a gauntlet for prisoners entering the camp to pass through and those prisoners were beaten by the policemen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: There was some partial cases, but only at the beginning. Only until such a regime and such criteria were introduced that whoever tried to do anything without being ordered was removed from his position and replaced by somebody else who was able to do their job properly. That was exclusively their idea. It was their initiative, the initiative of some individuals. They guided themselves with other considerations. It was their neighbours who knew who had had weapons and so on and so forth. But we removed those who behaved in violation of the regulations, but we removed them and finally there were no such cases left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you said when you testified before the state court in 2011, that the situation I described to you was actually a common practice. It happened, unfortunately, in your words, often.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I pointed out that it may have be common practice but at the beginning, while the people were frustrated, the very police officers providing security. You must bear in mind that some of their relatives may have been killed or massacred, and then they would avenge themselves. But we didn't know who these people were, because it wasn't written all over them. We first -- when we identified them, we looked at people who were able to carry out their duties properly, but it was certainly not anything permanent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also had confidential sources in the camp, because you're a security operative. You had confidential sources who told you that prisoners were being physically abused; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Through our sources we came up with the names of the perpetrators of these crimes, because we considered them crimes too, right there. And we singled them out, we suspended them, and replaced them. And you know what they got as a reward when they left Manjaca? They had to go to the front line to fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you yourself saw when prisoners were brought in for interviews, that they showed signs of having been physically beaten. You saw it too.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. Often they would say that they had fallen down upon arriving, and that's why they were bloody. But we were professionals and were able to conclude that the one who had brought them couldn't do so anymore, and he didn't. He was replaced by somebody else who was able to do the job in a more professional manner and with less emotion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your written evidence that people who were responsible for perpetrating these beatings were dismissed, you mean they were simply transferred away to other duties? On the front line, for example.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't a transfer. It was like a punishment. But the ones who were suspended, who had committed criminal acts, they were even taken by their police to military prison. And they weren't allowed to touch weapons again and couldn't contact other soldiers, those who had been -- who were known to have committed the offences that I described in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's talk about sort of disciplinary measures then for a minute. But let's leave these stories of these beatings aside for the time being. Mr. Radinkovic, you know, the -- the death by suffocation of the prisoners in the trucks who were coming from Sanski Most to Manjaca is one of the charges that Dr. Karadzic is faced with. All right? And the killing of a number of men in front of Manjaca camp on their arrival to the camp from Omarska is another one of the charges he stand indicted with, and you talked about both of these in your statement. Those happened, right? You confirm that these people, 24 men from Sanski Most and a number of men from Omarska were killed in the transportation to Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: As for Sanski Most, it was possible to establish that during the transport they suffocated. Nobody killed them. They simply suffocated because they were brought there in trucks with closed tarpaulins, and there were very many of them on one truck, and they simply suffocated because there wasn't enough air. These weren't killings that anyone committed. These were simply the circumstances. Somebody wasn't considerate enough to provide for enough air so that these people could arrive alive. As for transfers from Omarska, unfortunately this happened immediately in front of the camp gate, and it is obvious that these acts were committed by the police officers from the escort who had brought the prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these people who were killed, you knew about it on both occasions because you were on duty. You reported those killings up your chain of command, so your immediate superior, your camp commander, you all knew about it? In fact, you knew about these killings go on while they happened; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the same moment. Because the office where I was, is at some distance. But the commander of security was informing me of what was going on in front of the camp as far as Prijedor is concerned. And as for Sanski Most, I was informed because during the unloading of the healthy people, it was established that among them there were some dead people. Military police officers were there, and in such cases we insisted that the dead bodies would be taken back. We didn't want any dead bodies in front of our camp. And as for Prijedor, when I was informed that the killing of some individuals had begun, I even requested the help of the military police to prevent a possible -- I wanted to prevent that it grows out of proportion because the process had begun and I wanted to put an end to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to these two incidents that we are talking about, it's correct, isn't it, that the camp commander, Colonel Popovic, and the corps command, General Talic, neither man took any measures against the people who were under his -- their command who stood by and who watched while these things were going on, who failed to intervene? That no specific measures were taken either by your camp commander or by your corps commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: I must inform you that the camp was a military camp. That is, the military provided security. And the civilian structures brought the people. The civilian police, that is. Neither the camp commander nor General Talic had any direct influence. We equated them along the lines of command, but in neither -- or, rather, in both cases it was the civilian police that brought the people. Not the military. None of them was in a position to issue orders. We could only report up to the corps command and request that police station so-and-so be informed or the chief of police, whoever, so that the people be returned, the people who were brought dead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. [In English] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 30, from line 19 on, it was not recorded that the witness said, "I wanted to prevent what was happening because people had lost control." "The perpetrators had lost control," it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to add something to what the president has said. For that purpose, I personally made a phone call and requested urgent reinforcements because it was obvious that those people had the intention of committing perhaps even worse crimes. When a police platoon arrived with an armoured vehicle, things had already stopped, and then the process continued in line with the procedure, the way it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying now is you did something, you tried to do something. I was asking you about Colonel Popovic and General Talic. These incidents happened at the gate of the Manjaca farm. Manjaca was heavily guarded inside and outside by civilian and military police. There was a camp command structure inside. There was a guard house outside Manjaca from an elevated position where everything could be observed. There were armed guards all around the perimeter. Nobody intervened. Right? Apart from what you're telling us now, you did -- the staff at Manjaca camp stood by and let it happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Look here, the personnel of Manjaca camp had responsibility for security of the prisoners inside the camp but not outside it, and the guards were inside the camp, not outside. None of the police officers was allowed to go out, no matter what was happening. And once the police platoon had arrived with an armoured vehicle, it was clear that additional forces had been sent to prevent what could be prevented. If General Talic assigned it or any one of the commanders, it doesn't matter, but the reaction was as fast as possible because at that moment everything stopped and things began unfolding in accordance with the procedure that was applied in the camp in line with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're saying that because of the regulations, camp staff had no -- were not entitled, were not able, were not permitted to intervene to prevent a crime unfolding in front of their eyes? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. According to the orders, the security around the camp is provided by civilian police, and the military police has no right to intervene anywhere outside. The regulations were very strict: Outside security is provided by civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll assist in this. In the civil law generally that was applicable at the time, did a citizen not have a duty to intervene to prevent a criminal offence, whoever was committing it? That's a common provision in many jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: In civil law, yes, but military law is something different. So that this soldier who was standing at the gate and who was watching it happen, perhaps 20 or 30 metres away, he had his military duty to guard perhaps 2.000 people at that moment, whereas those who were outside were still not considered to be prisoners of war until they reached the gates of the camp. So there is a distinction. Perhaps that man wanted to intervene but he couldn't because his post, his work-place was to stand guard there, not outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And what about the military duty to protect civilians under the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what we did all the time in the camp, and the results are obvious, if we set aside these individual incidents. We did our utmost to achieve the maximum protection for civilians according to Geneva Conventions. Perhaps we did not succeed 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused. How does that square with what you said a moment ago about if a man wanted to intervene but couldn't because of his post? Are you suggesting that his post had primacy over the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the soldier who was part of the security detail inside the perimeter had the exclusive task to guard the people - that is to say, prisoners of war - who are inside the perimeter, not outside the perimeter. That is a clarification I want to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'll leave it there, but it doesn't resolve my confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just see it's 10.34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it time for morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 40 minutes. We'll resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, that will conclude my cross-examination. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The briefest possible, just one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radinkovic, picking up on the question put by Judge Morrison, can you tell us how many times killings happen in the vicinity of the camp, in the vicinity of that guard?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that happened only once when POWs from Prijedor were brought. It happened that once and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the balance of power between the military police guarding the camp and those outside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that's an appropriate question arising from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As far as duty to protect is concerned, I think there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the -- absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A jurisdictional matter may be raised. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic -- or can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask, was he able to intervene without the decision or order from his own superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's one question. And the other question is about the balance of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under what circumstances would a guard from the military police be able to intervene against the civilian police when that happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Only when the civilian police or any other unit attacked the camp, physically, militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One general question, Mr. Radinkovic. What do you know talk about conduct of the first superiors vis-à-vis identified perpetrators in your camp. Did they let it pass or did they react and how?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: The commanders of security, as they were known, did not allow physical violence against the prisoners, but of course they could not follow every policeman 24/7 or prevent any activity. So our security commanders often intervened without any orders from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radinkovic, for coming here and giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR RADINKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Radinkovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I was wondering if I could raise one matter in private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll bring in the next witness. I take it this will be the last witness for the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And I suppose that the Defence will be ready to work until 4.00 as yesterday if it is for the sake of completing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see how it goes. The parties prefer to do without tomorrow's hearing. That's the position. We'll see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miskovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I would like to take this opportunity to greet the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution as well, not only Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just leave a pause between questions and answers so that everything is recorded on the LiveNote, because we speak the same language. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D49034 is the document I would like shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the monitor. Please leave that pause that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see very well. Could this be made larger?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the first page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it is. Yes, I'm comparing them now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just don't start answering immediately. Leave one seconds' pause.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you we now show the witness the last page for him to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement reflect faithfully what you've said to the Defence team? Are there any inaccuracies that you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: There is one little thing, in fact, just a few errors that I would like to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please. Paragraph 10, last line, right after "municipal boards," it should say "and deputies."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I found it. "As far as I remember, the official suggestion of the leadership of the party was" --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: For the presidents of the Municipal Boards of the party as well the deputies should not be chairman or president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there anymore?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 12. It says that my municipality Prijedor was free and independent in its work from the republic organs at Pale. This a mistake, I think. The way it is phrased, you could understand that we are some renegade municipality working on its own. What I actually said or meant was that, in a certain period, we were unable to contact and communicate the leadership of the party, because there were no land-lines in one period and in another period telephone communications were down, too. So if it's understood to mean that, then it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I can also confirm that my municipality Prijedor ..."

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In the periods when there were no communications across land with the leadership of the party, it was physically impossible to reach them, and in the periods when telecommunications were down, we had to make our own decisions as far as the party is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. And there are some typos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taking into account these corrections you've just made, does this statement contain all that you have said to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, with these corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: My answers would be the same today as they were on the earlier occasions when I gave evidence because the truth is only one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson, could you assist us with regard to the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We are asking that four documents be admitted as associated exhibits. All of them have been on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some of them were already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I checked this morning and none of them have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit them all. Shall we assign numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement receives Exhibit Number D4206. The 65 ter number 1D26372 receives Exhibit Number D4207. The 65 ter number 13972 receives Exhibit Number D4208. The 65 ter number 1D25930 receives Exhibit Number D4209, and the 65 ter number 1D25938 receives Exhibit Number D4210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read in English a short summary of Mr. Simo Miskovic's statement. [In English] Simo Miskovic was the president of the SDS in Prijedor from 1991. Before he became the president of the SDS, he was in command of the reserve police station Prijedor 2. The SDS was a democratic party and decisions were taken at the Main Board sessions when the agenda was discussed and decisions were adopted and rejected by majority vote. There were conflicts between party policy and some representatives of the government at the municipal level, which is why these representatives were dismissed from their position and others were appointed to take their places. The basic policy adopted by the Municipal Board in Prijedor was presented by Mr. Miskovic on October the 5th, 1992. In his programme, Mr. Miskovic distanced himself and the party from all negative conduct in Prijedor municipality and requested that all responsible organs, each in its domain, take measures to prevent illegal actions in any segment and bring to the trial persons who committed them. When the SDS representatives in Prijedor became disobedient, Mr. Miskovic agreed with Dr. Karadzic to dismiss them, but part of the party leadership and the authorities refused to align with this decision. For this reason, Mr. Miskovic resigned and withdrew from the leadership of the party on 16th of August, 1993. Simo Miskovic was not aware of any plans to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from areas of BH to which the Bosnian Serbs laid claim, through genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and inhumane acts. He never heard such things in the Prijedor Municipal Board or at the sessions of the Main Board at the republican level. In Prijedor municipality, Mr. Miskovic contacted a large number of non-Serbs in order to find a peaceful resolution of the tensions in the area, and he proposed to the president of the SDA, Mirza Mujadzic, to visit together those places where Serbs and Muslims were concentrated, in order to reduce the tensions. For unknown reasons, Mr. Mujadzic refused. Mr. Miskovic was present at the meeting held at the Holiday Inn hotel on 14th of February, 1992. During this meeting, the instruction on organisation and work of the organs of the Serbian people in BiH in extraordinary circumstances were handed to participants. I suppose -- I apologise, I suppose it must be some mistake. It didn't happen 14th February, but we'll clarify it. The reason for this was in case of any danger to the survival of the Serbian people for the SDS representatives to take measures to prevent such attempts at a new slaughter. The local authorities in Prijedor municipality were free and independent of the republican organs in Pale, and it was clarified in what terms. The telephone lines had mostly been disrupted, and so for most part it was not possible the make contacts by telephone, and for that very reason, instructions from Pale could not be received. The crisis in Prijedor municipality was a consequence of the inability to reach an agreement between the representatives of the SDS, SDA, and HDZ political parties. A first meeting was held between the representatives of the three parties at which they agreed on the division of power in 50 per cent of the cases and scheduled another meeting for the next day to divide other 50 per cent of power. The next day, the SDA representatives did not show up, and after that, they no longer invested any effort into solving this problem. In Prijedor, there were no incidents on ethnic ground, because all three sides respected the agreement and acted accordingly, putting up check-points in settlement of ethnic concentrations. In this context, the three peoples kept in regular contact, talked, and maintained this situation. The first incident that took place was a murder of the reserve police officer Radenko Dzapa on 1st of May, 1992, then the killing and wounding of soldiers who were returning from the battle-field on Hambarine hill by Muslim paramilitary formation on 22nd of May, 1992, and the barricading of the Prijedor-Banja Luka main road by Muslim extremists. The inability to divide power created tensions among the three peoples because government could not function. In order to prevent incontrollable conflicts, the Serbs took over power in Prijedor on 30th of April, 1992. The culmination of the confrontations came after the attack on the town of Prijedor by Muslims and Croatian formations on 30th of May, 1992. The attack resulted in a large number of casualties among members of the Serbian people. And that is summary, and I have just to clarify one thing. [Interpretation] Excellencies, I believe that the date is wrong in the summary, but in the statement in paragraph 10 the date of that session at the Holiday Inn is correct, the 19th of December. So I don't have to ask the witness anything about that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been a long time, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's duly noted. And you have no question, no further questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. I'm saving time for the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Miskovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have P2571, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, in your statement you've made comments about the way the SDS party functioned and the nature of Dr. Karadzic's leadership; in particular, at paragraph 4 you state that the SDS was a democratic party. And in various places, you speak about democratic decision-making in the party. And I'd just like to address some of those comments you make with a concrete example. Now on the screen in front of you is a transcript of an intercepted conversation on the 10th of September, 1991, involving Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Neskovic, yourself, and Mr. Srdic. You've seen this intercept several times before, so I'm just going to go to a few extracts and ask you to confirm some of the things you've said before about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could first go to page 3 of the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And extract that I'd like you to look at starts at about halfway down the page in the B/C/S and it's near the top in the English. It's where Mr. Neskovic says: "Because they do not recognise any authority here, especially if you mention Sarajevo." And Dr. Karadzic says: "Let them fuck their mothers, let them make their own party, let them resign. Whoever refuses to obey Sarajevo should resign. Write papers for them tomorrow and say: This is a party which has its top and its bottom, and nobody will fuck about under our name." And when Dr. Karadzic speaks again, he says: "And please tell them this, please, whoever won't adhere to the policies of the party and implement the policies of the party, but adheres to their own private policies ..." And Neskovic says: "Yes." And Dr. Karadzic says: "... let them sign here, let them leave their place in the municipality, and we will put new people there. They can set up their own party but not under this name." Now basically what Dr. Karadzic is saying here is that party members must follow party policies or leave the party; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: This conversation took place before I came to head the party. This is the moment when I agreed after the fourth attempt that was made by certain representatives of the municipal organisation of the Serb democratic party to persuade me to accept to be at the helm of the party, because from the moment --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: -- when it was founded in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I asked a very specific question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We will go to other passages of this intercept. If I could ask you --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to please just answer the specific question that I just ask, which is: In the passage that I just read out to, Dr. Karadzic is stating that party members must follow party policies or leave the party; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what was read out to me, it seems that it is what was said to Neskovic. It was Neskovic who was told all of that. Not me. This is a conversation between Neskovic, who was a representative of the Main Board, who came to take care of the situation in the party before I came in. This is a conversation -- well, Srdjo Srdic, a member of parliament of the Serb Democratic Party, it's his department, and he was supposed to be replaced, and I was supposed to come to the helm. So this is a conversation between Neskovic and them. I was on the sidelines, if you will, and it was only towards the end that I communicated with Mr. Karadzic. So the conversation is between Neskovic, the member of the Main Board who was entrusted by the Main Board with this task of coming to the Prijedor to clarify the situation and to elect a new leadership of the party. So it's not between me And President Karadzic as far as I can understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you what you said before about this passage when you testified at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 25674.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In the Stanisic -- and page 25 of that exhibit. In the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, Mr. Miskovic, you were asked: "And Karadzic then continues and says: "'Whoever refuses to obey Sarajevo should resign. Write papers for them tomorrow and say this is a party which has its top and bottom and nobody will fuck about -- fuck under our name -- fuck about under our name.'" And you say: "Yes." And you were asked: "What do you think he meant by that?" And you answer: "I really don't know. You would have to ask him. As a layman, I would say that he is talking about the party policies and that everybody has to subscribe to those. Either you fall in or you leave, and that's the case all over the world. You can't be against the party and be a member of it." Now that's what you said about the passage of this intercept when you testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: As for what you read out just now, I fully stand by that. That is my statement and I confirm that just now. I just reacted to something else a moment ago. This conversation that you proffered, it's a conversation between Neskovic and President Karadzic, and what you are referring to now it's a conversation between myself and President Karadzic and that happened afterwards. And there is no denying that. And I believe that in all political parties in the world there is hierarchy, and the policy of the party has to be implemented. And if one doesn't want to implement that policy, then they have to join a different party. So there has to be order, there has to be hierarchy, and it has to be established that way. And primarily, the decisions of the Main Board, depending on how the party is organised. I mean, these bodies of political organisation. That is the basic thing. Who doesn't accept that? Well, then, you see often you have people who switch parties, who go from one party on another. They change their opinions and then they --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: -- join another party --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: First of all, you've been asked to speak more slowly. Secondly, I am asking very specific questions and your answers are straying away from them and my time is very limited. Mr. Miskovic, the testimony I just read out to you was your comment on the very same conversation between Mr. Neskovic and Mr. Karadzic that you looked at. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course that's the way it was. No denying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to P2571 to page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now why do I not see this in Serbian? I don't. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could just wait for a moment, Mr. Miskovic, the transcript will appear. And this is towards the bottom of the page in the English and also in the B/C/S, and this is part of the --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I see it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- towards the bottom of the page where you and Dr. Karadzic are speaking. And Dr. Karadzic says to you: "Good evening. Please tell me, was it the municipal assemblymen club that called the Assembly meeting tomorrow?" And you say: "Yes." And Dr. Karadzic says: "They don't have that prerogative, the motherfuckers." And you say: "Yes, probably the Main Board. They know -- I am not a member of the Main Board. The Main Board probably gave them carte blanche." And Karadzic says: "They cannot give them carte blanche. They are implementing the policies of the party, not the other way around." Now, when you testified previously about this passage, you explained that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am not sure we have right Serbian page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It should be page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand any of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As a matter fact, this is not the same. This is not proper document at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it's correct in the English. It should be page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you look at the B/C/S, the speakers are different.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that the document is incorrect in the B/C/S. I'm not -- oh, and -- yeah, I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in my e-court, I see Neskovic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, mine as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, this is towards the bottom of the page, you and Dr. Karadzic speaking, where you say to Dr. Karadzic: "The Main Board probably gave them carte blanche."
