And he says: "They cannot give them carte blanche. They are implementing the policies of the party, not the other way around." And when you testified previously about this passage, you explained that Dr. Karadzic was stating here that: "The SDS members and the Municipal Assembly are there to further party policies, and if they want to pursue other policies they have to change their party membership." That's a correct understanding of your view of this passage; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 12 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S. This is where Dr. Karadzic speaks with Mr. Srdic who was then the municipal party president. This is near the very top in the B/C/S and a about a third of the way down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic says to Mr. Srdic: "Srdja, please, what you just said is very bad. You are saying that you are going around and that you are a deserving man. We all know how deserving you are, but it's not working that way any longer, Srdja. You see, it's not working. The party is stuck. It's not working. You have to yield and let someone finish it." Now, what Dr. Karadzic is telling Mr. Srdic here is that he has to yield his position as municipal SDS president and let someone else take over. And you indeed became SDS president the next day and Mr. Srdic did not resist that change; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. I said at the very outset. All of this is happening in Mr. Srdic's apartment. He was the president of the party and also a member of a parliament too. He was an elderly man and younger people were against him. There was confrontation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then this person had some authority in Prijedor. So then they came to pick me up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speed, speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, you are speaking too fast. So could you repeat from where you said there was confrontation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I came to the helm of the party, in the party there were quite a few problems. The first president was Milakovic, Milorad, who behaved almost like a quack. So Srdja Srdic took over the party. He was a member of the party at the time on behalf of the Serb Democratic Party. Now this transcript, the conversation that has taken place there, it is in Srdja Srdic's apartment. I am present as the candidate for the future president, then member of the Main Board, Radomir Neskovic, and Srdja Srdic. His wife was there too, but she did not take part of this conversation, I mean. From the transcript, one can see that there is communication between the president of the party, Mr. Karadzic, and Srdja Srdic, as president of the municipal organisation of the Serb Democratic Party, and Neskovic, as a representative of the Main Board. I mean, one can see that it is geared towards the following: That there are problems in the party and that they have to be overcome through a new leadership. That is why Mr. Neskovic came in the first place. However, Srdja Srdic was hurt. He was saying: Well, I am not a ruin to be destroyed all together. However, after these conversations that were conducted with President Karadzic - and that is what is contained in this transcript - he finally understood that nobody was trying to destroy him or topple him. Rather, that in order to consolidate the party, it was necessary for a new man to be brought in who would have better communication with the membership of the party, since the majority were young people. And at that time, I was relatively young too. I was about 46 or 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miskovic. I think your position is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 6 of the English and page 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I do apologise. May I? May I just ask you to remind me to speak more slowly, because it is my nature to speak very fast and I tend to forget that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now on this page, Mr. Miskovic, right at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and towards the top in the English, again, this is you and Dr. Karadzic speaking. And Dr. Karadzic is saying that: "The assemblymen should be fair towards the party which brought them to power. You do this and don't -- there will be no conflicts, do it as a good housekeeper. There is no reason?" And then you state: "I wouldn't. You can ... I wouldn't do it because of you and the party, and since you are heading the party, because I know that it's a mess here, you have to figure everything out, and you have not only Prijedor, but the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, and loads of information every day, every month, from the elections to other things." Now you have stated previously that what you're saying here to Dr. Karadzic is that when you took over as party president, you would follow the policies of the SDS Main Board; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I wouldn't have accepted to lead the party if I were to pursue the policy of some other party.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 25675, page 22 in the English and page 32 -- sorry, 21 of the English and page 31 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the document that will be coming up, just to orient you, Mr. Miskovic, is transcript of your interview with the OTP in 2009. And this is right around the middle of the page in the B/C/S and towards the bottom of the page in the English, and you're discussing with the OTP this same intercept we've been looking at. And in fact, this same passage. And you're asked: "I've got one question, Mr. Miskovic. You say 'since you are heading the party,' was that your view that as head of the SDS he had the right to give instructions about what should happen?" And you say: "He was -- the Main Board of the SDS made decisions and he was the one representing the Main Board who was making the politics and the party on all levels was to conduct the policies, otherwise it would have been chaos. There was an Assembly and there was a Main Board. Later on, there was an Executive Board. I think Neskovic was on this Executive Board from 1993 or far away from it. I can't recall the little details right now." And on the next page of the English you're asked: "I understand that it's a long time ago, but just so I understand that answer, the Main Board made the policies. He was the representative of the Main Board as leader of the SDS." And if we turn the page in the B/C/S, you answer: "Yes, he was the first. Like in every party, the main body makes decisions. They confront their opinions in the main body, and he's controlling of the implementing of the decision." Now that accurately -- that passage I read out accurately summarised your understanding of Dr. Karadzic's authority within the SDS party; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is nothing there that is to be challenged. Any party has its bodies, and the president of the party only pursues the policy that is agreed upon by these bodies of the party, and he is responsible for the implementation of that policy. As far as I know, that is the characteristic of all political parties all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about the Variant A and B instructions. At paragraph 10, your statement indicates that you were asked whether you had information about the meeting at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo on 19 December 1991, at which the Variant A and B instructions were distributed. And you confirmed in your statement that you attended this meeting. The Chamber has received evidence that, in fact, this meeting took place on the 20th of December, 1991. An example would be P5792. Do you agree, Mr. Miskovic, that this meeting where the Variant A and B instructions were distributed could well have taken place on the 20th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I said even before, and I must repeat it now, that I do not remember the date. I do remember, though, a nice scene. When we finished, in the lobby of the Holiday Inn, I met Mirza Mujadzic, the president of the SDA party at Prijedor, and he was boasting to me of getting a new Golf car.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I'm very sorry to interrupt you, but my time is it very limited and I'm just asking --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again I'd like to confirm some things you said before about these instructions. Now, that meeting you attended in December 1991 where these instructions where distributed, that meeting was presided over by Dr. Karadzic and was attended by all municipal party presidents and National Assembly deputies; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I know that I attended, and my digression was only to -- meant to show how relaxed the atmosphere was still between us, that's why I provided that example. But okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What you said in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, and this is at page 39 in e-court of your -- of the transcript, was: "All party presidents were present at the meeting, as well as deputies in the National Assembly. The paper was distributed, and we were asked to act accordingly and to convey the instructions to the Municipal Boards and inform them about the existence of the two variants." Now that accurately reflects who was present and what happened at that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only confirm that I attended that meeting, that I received that document, that paper, and that I acquainted the Municipal Board with its contents. It was my policy to inform the Municipal Board of everything, and that's how it was throughout the time I was at the helm of that board.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender the page from which I just read out. It's page 39 of 65 ter 25674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 65 ter 25674, page 39. And it's the first full answer on that page, where it says: "Received those at the meeting at Sarajevo ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in English here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, just so you know, this is the passage I read out to you so it was translated to you in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were asked from whom you did receive these instructions and your answer: "Received those at a meeting in Sarajevo -- or, rather, in Pale, a meeting that we attended, but I can't be sure of the exact location. All party presidents were present at the meeting, as well as deputies in the National Assembly. The paper was distributed, and we were asked to act accordingly and to convey the instructions to the Municipal Boards and inform them about the existence of the two variants." Do you stand by that answer you gave in Stanisic and Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this page. Have we admitted it already? Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while we have this exhibit up, if we could go to page 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Miskovic, this is only in English. So I will read it to you. This is at the top of the page. You say: "Let me inform the Chamber so that the Chamber knows. The establishment of the Serbian Assembly was in case that they were supposed to take over power, in case we were supposed to secede, we had to have bodies that functioned already. They were not functioning. The joint bodies were still functioning so this was just the establishment of the Assembly according to Variant B and the Serbian presidents, and Serbian bodies were established and elected in case there was a cessation of the Serbian territories from the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We always wanted to have authorities in place and that's how they had been created and that's how they were composed of, from the cadre that has just been shown. The joint government still functioning properly at the time in question." Now that accurately describes the creation of the Serbian Municipal Assembly in Prijedor pursuant to Variant B and the purpose of that Variant A and B document in your view; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you have presented this to the Chamber accurately. I will repeat. It is true that on the 7th of January, 1992, I believe, we established a Serbian Assembly which existed on paper but did not function. The basic reason for its establishment was the following: In case of danger to the Serbs in the Prijedor municipality, and there were many indications that that might happen because it was not possible to divide power in the municipality, and that's situation had begun before I arrived. And therefore this shadow Assembly, if you will, was established, and after a month, an Executive Board was set up too. The members of the party and the members of the government had already been elected at local elections. Stakic was the president, only through his decision he was appointed president, conditionally speaking. And then there was Milan Kovacevic, who was president of the Executive Board remained in that position and so on. That's the essence. The essence is not that Bosnia and Herzegovina could secede as you said. This was a local issue. In the territory of the Prijedor municipality, in this way a Serbian municipality was established, and we didn't obstruct the two other ethnicities to establish their own municipalities where they constitute the majority of the population. In this way, we thought that we could avoid confrontation and conflict in that area. So this didn't have to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole but is limited to the Prijedor municipality, where the Serbs were the majority. And we still haven't discussed the reasons for taking power, but I believe the time will come for us to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 25 of page 60 and in the following lines, it was not recorded that the witnesses said: "In the territory of Prijedor municipality to establish a Serbian municipality and the Serbian territories."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the areas where the Serbs were the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, what you said in your previous testimony was that purpose of Variant A and B document was to establish Serbian bodies in the event there was a cessation of Serbian territories from the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the purpose of the Variant A and B instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know that what I have just said is not in contradiction to what I said earlier. This is the truth. I doubt that it was different earlier, because we could not exert influence on politics at BH level. We were at the local level and we -- all our activities were also local. I'm talking about the Prijedor municipality and, consequently, the Serbian municipality of Prijedor; that is, the area where the Serbs were the majority. That's what I meant. And this is also the context in which we have to understand this cessation, as far as I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page as well, please, to be added to P6587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, you attended in February of 1992 an extended session of the SDS Main Board in Sarajevo where Dr. Karadzic activated stage 2 of the Variant A and B instructions, and you passed on that instruction from Dr. Karadzic to the Prijedor Municipal Board; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. When I received the paper with Variants A and B at the Holiday Inn, after returning to Prijedor I acquainted the members of the Municipal Board with that paper. This can be found in the minutes somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: All documents were seized when IFOR --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you again because now you're going back to December of 1991. You said you don't remember. I'm going to show you the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P5516, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the SDS Prijedor Municipal Board of the 17th of February, 1992. And you can see right after the number -- the word "agenda" and there is a number 1 which says: "Briefing on the meeting of the Main Board and the Serbian Assembly of BH." And then it says that: "After adopting the agenda, Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS Municipal Board, gave a briefing on the meeting held in Sarajevo." And the first thing you're recorded as saying is that Mr. Karadzic, President of SDS BH, was the main speaker. "It is an act of cessation of the BH, on the part of the SDA. In that respect, we are forced to create national communities on ethnic territories." And if we could move down in the English and go to the next page in the B/C/S, about three or four lines in the B/C/S there is an asterisk and you're recorded as stating: "Serbs shall not participate in any way in the referendum conducted by the SDA. In view of that, it is necessary to activate the second stage of the position stated by the SDS BH Main Board." Now, these minutes reflect you transmitting Dr. Karadzic's instructions not to participate in the referendum and to implement the second stage of the Variant A and B instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: My request to you would be if we could just return to this document and reread it. It was a long time ago. I'm not so familiar with the context. If I could just once more.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was: These minutes reflect you transmitting to the Municipal Board Dr. Karadzic's instructions, both the instruction not to participate in the referendum and the instruction to implement the second stage of the Variant A and B instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that at that meeting or at any meeting, for that matter, although I may have forgotten, that the main -- that at the Main Board session was -- there were ever suggestions to act in accordance with Variants A or B. Only in the event of danger to the Serbian people in any given area. That is true, for sure. But I don't remember all directives. In general, I remember that it was this way. If this is an original and if this was discussed there -- does this bear my signature, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, maybe we can shortcut it by -- I can put what you said previously about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25674 again, please, at page 48.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And since it's only in English, I'll begin reading it while it's coming up. And you're being asked about these same minutes I just showed you and you're asked: "The minutes that we're looking at, sir, say or report that it's necessary to activate the second stage of the position stated by the SDS BH Main Board; namely, Variant A and B at this time. Do you accept that at this meeting --" And you answer: "Variant B, yes." And you're asked: "Do you accept that at this board meeting the conclusion was made to activate the second stage of Variant B by the Prijedor Municipal Board?" And this is at the bottom of the page, you say: "You mean, was that a decision by the Municipal Board at the time," over to the next page, "that work should be done on the activities of Variant B? Is that what you mean? If that's what you mean, then yes, preparations." Now it's correct, as you stated in your previous testimony, that at the Prijedor Municipal Board meeting, the minutes of which we just looked at, the decision was taken to begin activating the stage 2 of the Variant A and B instructions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I have just confirmed that the Municipal Board decided about that. I don't remember that the Main Board or the leadership of the party decided about that; whereas the Municipal Board, yes, it did decide about that and a Serbian Assembly and an Executive Board were established. Both shadow bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have P12, please. Page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, this is a recording of the 14th of February, 1992, extended session of the Main and Executive Boards. Right at the bottom of page 5 in the English, and near the middle of the page 4 in the B/C/S, and this is all Dr. Karadzic speaking, he says: "That is, if you remember, who keeps that in mind, or maybe not on his person, a stage number 2. There is, remember," and then the next page in the English, "you know what I am talking about. We know, yes, that is therefore the stage number 2, the second stage, in smaller or bigger variations, but you have to implement that slowly now, to have absolute control who is travelling along your roads, what they are transporting, for which purposes. That's the way it must be." Now, Mr. Miskovic, this is Dr. Karadzic's first reference at this meeting to -- where he instructs municipal representatives to activate stage 2 of the Variant A and B document; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember this document, nor do I remember this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 7 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. And this is about a third of the way down in the B/C/S and it's about -- starts about five lines down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic says: "We must not participate in the referendum. Everything they do without us is of no use." And about five lines down, he says: "The second thing that is very important, it gives us full moral right not to accept any decision resulting from the referendum, and it gives us right to introduce the stage number 2 in functioning of your areas and relying on your own forces to absolutely defend yourself from the independent Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is Dr. Karadzic's second reference to the need to implement stage 2 of the Variant A and B document at this meeting. Do you remember that one?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I said a minute ago that I don't remember this document at all and I don't remember the conversation, either. It's a fact, however, and it's beyond dispute, that the whole Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina was against the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the former Yugoslavia. And in that context, later on a referendum was carried out. So it's beyond dispute that all the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were against Bosnia-Herzegovina seceding from Yugoslavia, because they thought that they would be jeopardized by that way as a collective body.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll show you one more passage from this meeting, and it's at page 17 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S. I'm not sure if it's just my problem, but my e-court screen is now black. I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably it's time to take a break. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.15. I have been told that we cannot go beyond 3.00 due to a Status Conference, which takes place in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, as I mentioned before the break, I'd like to show you one last passage of this 14 February 1992 Main Board meeting where Dr. Karadzic speaks at length. And that's on the page before you. It's towards the bottom of the page in your language, about two-thirds of the way down. And it's right near the middle in the English. And he says: "I think that we Serbs must stop with declarations -- with declaration. We've had enough declarations. And now those declarations should be translated into a map. And the stage number 2 should also be converted. The one we've talked about, the one you have, if not here, then at home, in order to -- in order to" --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see this -- oh, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "... in order to have authorities in the field functioning, that a bird cannot fly over, really." I take it from your earlier answers, Mr. Miskovic, that you also have no recollection of this, the third mention Dr. Karadzic makes at this meeting of activating stage 2? You don't remember attending any such meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I said already I don't remember this meeting at all. I'm not saying it didn't take place. I'm just saying I have absolutely no memory of it. As for the implementation of the Variant B, I've already said that we had made that decision. We informed the Municipal Board, and we later established the Serbian Assembly, et cetera, as per Variant B. But I don't really remember this meeting. It was 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 14, the witness said: "We established the Serbian Assembly and the shadow Executive Board."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 05721, page 23 of the English and page 25 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 65 ter 05721, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I was just showing you the transcript of the 14 February 1992 extended meeting of the Main Board held at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo. Now this --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I need page 25 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a Holiday Inn receipt in your name reflecting your stay at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo on the night of the 14th and 15th of February, 1992, "to be paid for the hotel services for members of the SDS Assembly." That's your holiday -- that's a Holiday Inn receipt in your name reflecting your attendance at the meeting, the transcript of which we just looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I never said, now or before, that I did not attend this meeting, and I did receive the papers about Variant A and B. I don't see where the problem is now. It's true that I spent the night at the Holiday Inn. It's true that I attended the meeting. It's true that I received that paper describing Variants A and B. And it's true that upon return to Prijedor, I informed the Municipal Board thereof and it's true that we later formed the Serbian Assembly and the shadow Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I think you're confused. You're now talking again about December 1991. I am talking about the 14 February 1992 meeting, the transcript of which I just showed you, at which Dr. Karadzic activated stage 2 of the Variant A/B instructions which you already had. And this Holiday Inn receipt reflects your attendance at that meeting on the 14th of February, 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not confused. I'm confused only insofar that according to this, and you'll confirm this, it seems that I was at the Holiday Inn twice, but I was -- I stayed there only once, and that's when I received that Variant A and B paper. It's possible that this meeting took place, but I don't remember it. I remember only the other one. It's not disputed that I stayed at the Holiday Inn, that I took that paper. Are you staying that I stayed at the Holiday Inn twice, on the 14th and some other date? I don't know about that. I was there only once as far as I remember, if memory serves me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page of this 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6588, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, at paragraph 14 of your statement you talk about the SDS take-over of power in Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992, and you describe it as something that was intended to ease rising tensions and ensure peace. Now, however you may have viewed that, you would agree, wouldn't you, that it is highly unlikely that the Muslims and Croats of Prijedor viewed the unilateral take-over of power of the democratically elected government in Prijedor by the SDS as a move that would ease ethnic tensions. They would have seen that as a provocative move that would have added to the ethnic tensions at the time, no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the take-over is concerned and the tensions that existed and that were caused in a way by the take-over, this Court should know that the problem in Prijedor, when I came to be the head of the party, from the very beginning was the division of power after the multi-party elections. I'm saying this because you just mentioned that the take-over could have caused tensions on the other side. If you put it that way, then one could conclude that obstruction and shirking from the division of power after the multi-party elections was on the part of the SDA because they covered all the important posts in Prijedor municipality so that out of ten senior posts --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I appeal to the Chamber that witness would be allowed to accomplish his own response.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I didn't ask for a history of what happened in Prijedor after the multi-party elections. I asked a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, would you agree that the Muslims and Croats of Prijedor on the whole viewed the SDS's unilateral take-over of power on the 30th of April, 1992, as a provocative move that inflamed ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to show you that it was not what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Miskovic, your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. But I didn't want to give such a terse answer. I wanted to explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson may ask why. Wait for the question, please. Please continue please, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have D31830, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, these are the 23rd of April, 1992, SDS Municipal Board meeting minutes. And you're clearly present because it says you opened the meeting. And if you could look at number 5 in the list of decisions, it says: "To immediately start working on the take-over, the co-ordination with the JNA notwithstanding." When you were shown this document previously and this particular point in your prior testimony, you said that this reflects the fact that the SDS was preparing to take-over power, and that if the JNA was not willing to do it, you would carry it out with armed Serb reserve soldiers and police; correct? That's what number 5 here reflects.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In item 5 it says, "Start work immediately on the take-over regardless of co-ordination with the JNA." My signature is missing from this. I don't know where you found this record. All the records were kept in longhand. I have them at home. But it's indisputable that in keeping with Variant B we had the intention of using this corps in Prijedor municipality to take over and thus prevent a pogrom. And you could see that during the take-over, there were no unfortunate events until the -- until what happened later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 9, it's missing: "In the event of danger, we take measures to prevent a pogrom." "Danger to the Serbian people," the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, again, if you could please answer directly my question. Do you agree that point 5 of these minutes reflect the SDS position at the time, that they were preparing to take over power and that if the JNA was not willing to do it, you would carry it out with armed Serb reservists and police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: This is taken out of context. A moment ago you did not let me explain the fear from the other side --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: -- in case of take-over. I wanted to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to enable you to see the fear on the other side, why the Serb side was forced to carry out this take-over. It's difficult for you to understand what happened in the area of Prijedor and Kozara, but in another testimony I explained it. In the Second World War, that region saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- saw a huge loss of life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- we won't go there. Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, if I could have 65 ter 25674, page 84, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Miskovic, I am going to read out what you said in your prior testimony when you were shown point 5 of this document. You were asked: "And finally with this document, sir, number 5, there is a conclusion" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are we on correct page?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, it should be page 84.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no Serb version of the transcript at the International Tribunal. She will read out and then you can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "And finally with this document, sir, number 5" --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- "there is a conclusion or a decision, sorry, to immediately start working on the take-over. Do you see that?" "A. Yes, yes. "Q. And what did that mean? "A. Well, you know what that meant. It meant that certain preparations had to be made because the blockade was still ongoing in order to take over power. Something had to happen there. We had to let the water out, conditionally speaking. In that sense, that is what it means. There were armed soldiers in the JNA. If the JNA was not willing to do it, then we would take the Serb soldiers, and then in the police we would have the policemen and the reserve forces, so from both sources we had armed people, and in that way we would protect the Serbian people. So it was in that sense, and that's what actually was -- that's actually what happened later." That's what you said in your previous testimony in relation to the document I just showed you and that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not disputing that we were working to organise and prepare the people -- I mean, that was the time when the JNA still existed. But when the JNA was disbanded, all the Serb soldiers and all able-bodied Serb men who had been engaged in the TO back in 1991, they were the ones who were supposed to protect the Serb people in Prijedor municipality. That's the context in which you should understand this, and in that context it's not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd tender this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Miskovic, again, I'd like you to please listen to my questions and answer my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, a few minutes ago when I asked you about this -- the minutes regarding the -- with the mention of the taking over of power, you said that: "... it's indisputable that in keeping with Variant B we had the intention of using this corps in Prijedor municipality to take over and thus prevent a pogrom." And I'd just like to confirm that you did consider the take-over -- the SDS take-over on the 30th of April was part of your implementation of Variant B of the Main Board instructions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't get the beginning, the beginning of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's correct that you considered the SDS take-over of power on the 30th of April to be part of your implementation of Variant B of the Variant A/B instructions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 12 of your statement, you explain that there was a certain period of time in which you could not receive instructions from Pale, and earlier in your testimony today you mentioned the time when there wasn't a corridor. Now you did attend the 12th of May -- you attended the 12th of May, 1992, RS Assembly session in Banja Luka, where Dr. Karadzic announced the strategic objectives. You were at that session; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably. I don't remember the date. But if I was invited as president of the party, then I certainly went. But I don't remember the date or the discussion or the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 25629, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just wondering if this was notified to us to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It was certainly meant to be. I can double-check.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, this is a summary of the 18 May 1992 SDS Municipal Board meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'm just informed that it's my omission. I neglected to notify this document. I hope it doesn't cause any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's no problem, Mr. President, but it's nice that it happens once in a while on your side instead of always on our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And agenda item 2 says: "Report from the session of the Serbian Republic of BH Assembly." And if you look down at number 2, it says: "A report on the Assembly session was presented by President S Miskovic." And it says there were 18 items on the agenda, "the main guidelines in future activities were identified. Commander of the army supreme staff appointed, members of the Presidency of the Republic elected, et cetera." Now, does this remind you of the fact that you attended the 12 May 1992 RS Assembly session at which Dr. Karadzic announced the strategic objectives and then you passed on information from that session to the SDS Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you this: I went to all the meetings to which I was invited as president of the party in Prijedor. However, 20 years later, I don't remember the agendas or the discussion or the conclusions. Now I'm looking at this agenda but I don't remember it at all. And I don't know what to say. But I'm not questioning that I attended all the meetings to which I was invited or the sessions of the Main Board. I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this document reflects your attendance at an RS Assembly session, and the contents of what's stated here, in particular the appointment of the Main Staff commander and the members of the Presidency, indicate that that was in fact the 16th Session held on the 12th of May. Do you have any reason to doubt that you were, in fact, at that session and then reported back to the Prijedor SDS about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I said to you a moment ago, if I was invited to sessions, then I was certainly present because I was never absent. I thought it was my duty and obligation to attend in view of the position that I held. And it certainly was that way if that is what is written in the minutes, that that is how I informed the Municipal Board. But at this moment, I cannot remember the agenda, the discussion, or the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6589, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, at paragraph 14 of your statement you discuss the attack on the town of Prijedor by Muslim and Croat formations on the 30th of May, 1992. And you state that this attack "cast a shadow over all previous agreements and activities that had ensured peace in Prijedor." Now --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You are ignoring the fact that prior to the 30th of May, in the days preceding that, the VRS carried out major shelling and infantry attacks on the Muslim villages of Hambarine and Kozarac, shelling Muslim homes and killing and rounding up inhabitants of those villages. Now, there was no peace in Prijedor in the days prior to the 30th of May, 1992, was there? The Muslim population was already under attack.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it's the other way around, actually, and this is why. First of all, after the take-over of Prijedor, take a look at this, there was not single incident. No shops were broken. There were no conflicts between national structures. Communication was regularly maintained between and among all three ethnicities, all the way up until the first attack, when the Serb policeman Dzapa was killed. And then his uncle took revenge against these innocent Muslims who were on a bus coming from Zagreb. Then there was this attack when soldiers were ambushed by the Muslim forces on the way from Hambarine. They killed two or three soldiers, I cannot remember anymore, and wounded a few. Then the army reacted. Also, the Prijedor-Banja Luka road was blockaded, although we had previously agreed on free communication, that there would be free communication in all directions. So there was a reaction after these incidents. It was not just a capricious thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in fact after the shelling of Kozarac, you went to Kozarac and you saw homes and buildings that had been destroyed by the shelling; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not in Kozarac up until the after the end of war. I haven't been Mrakovica yet either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25674, please, page 104.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the very bottom of the page, the last question, it says: "When did you go back to Kozarac?" And this is in English, so I'll read it to you. And on the next page you answer: "For the first time? For the first time, it was after the shelling. I think I reached Dera. And not again for a long time. "Q. And this was -- this was a town that you knew well. What did you receive when you arrived there, after the shelling? "A. Well, I saw some houses and buildings destroyed by the shelling." Now, that's what you said when you testified previously and that's true, isn't it, Mr. Miskovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having reminded me. It is true that after the shelling -- well, it was in a private capacity because the party was banned, but never mind. I remember I got not mosque there. Yes, you have reminded me just now. And I saw that part of the houses were, I mean, damaged. But that is just this one time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 15 you briefly mention your visit to Omarska. You state that Mico Kovacevic invited you to visit the camp with him. And again, I'd like to remind you about some of the things you've said previously about this visit and ask you to confirm them. First, your visit to Omarska was together with a group of officials from Banja Luka and Prijedor, including Radislav Brdjanin, Stojan Zupljanin, Mico Kovacevic, and Milomir Stakic; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In the other statements I have already told you that it so happened that I was in front of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor when there was this jeep on the main road, and then Mico Kovacevic came up. And I cannot remember, you say that Stakic was there, too. Probably he was. I don't know. But as for Mico, we've known each other for a long time because his older brother lives in my neighbourhood and I know him from the days when we were students. And Mico came up, and he asked me to come along, and I said where are you going. And he said they came from Banja Luka and we are going to Omarska, and that's how I went along.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25675, page 66 of the English and page 102 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I interrupted you because I was just asking you who you went with, and I will show you what you said before about this now, because it appears you don't recall.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that I went and it's a fact that Mico invited me. And who else was there, I don't know. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could just wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It should be page 66 in the English, page 102 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were asked right around the middle of the page: "You actually went to Omarska in the company of Predrag Radic, didn't you?" And you answer: "A number of them." And you're asked: "Let's go through them. And you say: "Yes." "Radoslav Brdjanin? "Yes. "Stojan Zupljanin? "Yes. "Who else? "Mico Kovacevic, Stakic. "Who else was there? "There were other people from Banja Luka." So it's correct, is it not, that among the people you visited Omarska with were Brdjanin, Zupljanin, Kovacevic, and Stakic, no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, and I've stated that already on each and every occasion, that I was in Omarska on that day. And I told you about the way I went there. I do not remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could please just answer the question. If you don't remember who you went with, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Right now I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could tender this page. I don't believe any of this interview has an exhibit number yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 68 of the English and page 104 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just above the middle of the page in the English and towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, you're asked: "Was it clear to you that the people you saw in the camp had been ill-treated?" And you said: "I could see that they looked ill or looked bad, but I couldn't see what the treatment was since I wasn't there." Now that's correct, isn't it, you could see that the detainees looked ill and looked bad when you visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I said, I mean during the previous conversation, and I confirm that now, I just passed by these people who were standing on the other side of the fence, and I went to these steps that were on the left-hand side and we went to that room. I, I mean, cannot say who looked which way physically, who looked sick or who did not look sick. I think I just said that some of them had beards and I couldn't recognise them, therefore, and I am sure that they all recognised me because they knew me from before, you know. But I could not recognise anyone because I -- although I did pass nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I add this page to P6590, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 63 of the English and page 97 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is near the top of the page in both languages, and you're asked: "The people in those camps, Keraterm and Omarska, included women, didn't they? Or at least Omarska did?" And you answered: "Yes, I saw women when I first went there, and among them even my colleague Sifeta [phoen], I can't remember her family name." And that's correct as well, isn't it, Mr. Miskovic, you saw women among the detainees at Omarska when you went there; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Miskovic, not Misetic. It is true that I saw my colleague from work there, Sifeta, I forgot her last name. And I kept saying -- well, I never said that that was camp because, for me, that was an investigation centre. And I explained why I considered that to be an investigation centre. Because people were being investigated by the police, public, secret --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: -- professionals, that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, you're straying away from the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I'd like to go now to page 69 of the English and page 106 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I saw Sifeta there, my colleague.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection in relation to the camps. In the question, it says "camp," but the witness is commenting on the fact that he did not accept that that was a camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For no reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I explained the reasons why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question and we can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: He was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And near the top of the page in the English and towards the middle of the B/C/S, you state: "We climbed a staircase at this building." And a few lines down you say: "And as far as I remember, they were singing Serb or Chetnik songs." And you're asked: "Weren't you surprised that the Bosniaks and Croats were singing Serb songs?" And you say: "Yes, I was. Someone made them to." And I understand that in the B/C/S you also say: "It was obvious." Now that's correct as well, isn't it, Mr. Miskovic, when you and the others visited Omarska, the detainees were forced to sing Serb or Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were forced. I did hear that, but I was not present when somebody was forcing them to do that, if that happened in the first place. But I did hear them sing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would add this page to P6590, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, at paragraph 15, and again in your -- just a moment ago you stated that Omarska was an investigation centre. And in your statement you said that's what you believed because professional MUP officials were engaged in interrogating the prisoners. But isn't it true that at the time you actually questioned this label "investigation centre" because it wasn't clear to you how so many people could be allegedly investigated yet not a single charge brought against any of them? Isn't that what you thought at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: As regards that, I mean my opinion is very well known. I've already explained the reason why I think this was an investigation centre. However, as president of the party, and the work of the party was frozen, nobody informed me about the procedures there and whether there were proceedings instituted and whether somebody was punished, sentenced, et cetera, I really don't know about that. But those carrying out the investigations in the area do know. If there are no criminal reports or criminal charges or other charges -- I mean, I would just be surprised as a professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 22182, please. And if we could go to page 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, this is a transcript of an audio-recorded interview you gave the Prosecution back in 2001, and we only have an English transcript, so I'm going to read out a passage of that to you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In the middle of the page you are asked: "You must be aware, surely, that the detention camps were set up in Prijedor municipality?" And you answer: "No, it was like this as far as I know, as far as I was informed. I am telling you now the way I found out about it as an ordinary citizen, because the party was not operational, the work, the activities of the party were frozen. The information that I have was that collection centres and investigation centres were established. Investigation centre being one in Omarska. But I know one thing because fair number of my colleagues from the police was engaged in investigating people there, that is why I thought, I mean, why this was confirmed to me that this was investigation. But comment after everything was that, I said it wasn't clear to me, as I was policeman, that so many people being investigated but no charges were brought against them. There was not a single charge." Now, that's what you said in 2001 and that reflects your questioning of the label of Omarska as an investigation centre because not a single charge was brought against any detainee; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said I don't know whether charges were brought or were not brought. Nobody informed me officially. But I'm just saying to you as a professional, if - if - no charges were brought, then that is not clear to me. But I don't know. I wasn't functioning in that way at the time, and nobody had the duty to inform me in any way about that. I just got this information as an ordinary citizen, as the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would tender this page of this interview, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, at paragraph 13 you state that you only later learned about the Keraterm investigation centre. But you did know about the existence of Keraterm when it was operational, didn't you, because you heard about the massacre of prisoners there shortly after it happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that I do remember this thing happened. I was returning from Banja Luka - and I don't know why I went to Banja Luka - and at the crossroads in Cirkin Polje, the police were standing there and they were blocking the main road, and I said: What's going on? And they said there are some problems there. And I thought that perhaps there was a traffic accident. And they said there are some problems and we have to go in a different direction. And then I did go in a different direction, and I found out that certain unfortunate things had happened in Keraterm. That's when I founded out about that. After all, at the time I was -- I mean, I had a relationship with a certain lady and her brother was there at the time, so I heard from him about this thing that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In fact, you had a relationship with a certain Muslim lady. She had relatives in Keraterm, and you heard from her that there had been a massacre of prisoners there; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Allegedly, yes, a certain number of people had lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you know now that that was true; right? There were almost 200 people massacred one night in Keraterm. You know that now to be true, don't you? You said "allegedly."

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know. I don't know to this day. This is the first time I hear this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25674, page 169, please. Oh, sorry, just one other question on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, it's true that you did not do anything to try to find out what action was being taken against the people that had committed that alleged crime; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know on what basis I, as an ordinary citizen, could take action and interfere in the work of others, especially armed persons at the time. The work of the party was frozen at the time, so I operated like any other ordinary citizen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I take it that you agree you didn't do anything to find out what -- what was being done to investigate that crime or bring the perpetrators of the alleged crime to justice?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not in charge of that. There are services and organs that are in charge of doing that. Whether they did implement that or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 169 of 65 ter 25674, please. This should be page 169. I think we need to move forward three pages. One more page, please. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'm going to read to you what you said, a passage from your prior testimony, and this is about two-thirds of the way down this page. You said: "I was invited to come to the corps command because I often reacted to the looting and other crimes such as smuggling and so on, so people from the region would be summoned to come to the corps command to find out what's going on. And then the issue was raised how it's possible that the trucks can go through all the 50 check-points from our territory to Serbia, whereas I cannot even take a pin through these check-points." Now, what you were describing here, as I understand it, is that on one occasion you went to the 1 KK Corps command and complained about looting and smuggling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in relation to this, because I often reacted to that kind of thing at the Municipal Board and also on a private basis as a private individual, I was asked to come to the corps command and also other representatives of that subregion. They asked us to say who these people were. Who, I mean, did that. But I said: I mean how is it that you don't know them? I think that's what I said. There are about 50 check-points from here to Serbia and I, conditionally speaking, cannot get a needle through that way, and now you're asking me whose trucks these were. So this is it to the best of my recollection in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So as I understand it, you were complaining that trucks with looted goods could go through all 50 check-points between Prijedor and Serbia but you couldn't take anything at all through these check-points. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: These were not looted goods. This was a case of illegal trade. I mean, at the time when other young people were getting killed. That's the context. Because I don't know who was transporting what in trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said: "I often reacted to the looting and other crimes such as smuggling and so on, so people from the region would be summoned to come to the corps command to find out what's going on." Now you agree, do you not, that the discussion you had at the corps command was about looting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not initiate that. They called me to ask me why I was reacting that way. And it wasn't only me. It was also from Dubica and Novi, people from there, I think. And we've said what I've already told you about. I said that I could not get a needle through 50 check-points, and trucks and trailer-trucks could go through these check-points and now you're calling me to ask me who these people are. I am not checking them, I'm not checking the goods that they were transporting. I, as a citizen, simply see the reaction of people, and as a normal person I have to say that. I mean, while young people are getting killed. I just have to react to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Miskovic, it's just not a hundred per cent clear to me and I would just like you to confirm if you could with a yes or a no. The discussion you had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because given that the witness doesn't understand English and there's no B/C/S version, probably when you read the transcript read from the question and that's -- so that the witness can follow. This was a question whether you visited the Krajina Corps when Mr. Subotic visited Prijedor with Zupljanin, et cetera. So this is your answer. I quote: "I was invited to come to the corps command because I often reacted to the looting and other crimes such as smuggling and so on, so people from the region would be summoned to come to the corps command to find out what's going on. And then the issue was raised how it is possible that trucks can go through all the 50 check-points from our territory to Serbia, whereas I cannot even take a pin through those check-points." Do you remember having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The context is the following: We -- you have stated all the elements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but the context is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can answer -- start your answer with "yes" or "no" and then you can explain. Do you remember having said so, Mr. Miskovic? That's your testimony in Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's true. It's true. But the sequence how things went, I was also invited. I didn't go there of my own accord. Although, it would have been better if I had reacted of my own initiative but that's how it was anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue. Shall we add that page?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- would be a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, if I could just get you to answer, if possible, with a "yes" or a "no," this discussion at the corps command involved the subject of looting and smuggling. I'm not asking you what was said. Just that that was the topic or at least one of the topics discussed at that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can repeat today that I was invited there. I reacted immediately when I was asked who those people were. I reacted in the same way that I talked to you, and I was interrupted. But I couldn't put it differently. I said: How is it that I can't take a pin through these check-points, whereas others drove entire trailer-trucks through? And I received no answer but, of course, he wasn't obliged to give me one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 21740, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, at paragraph 6 and 16 of your statement, you discuss the conflict you have with municipal officials in Prijedor, which resulted in you threatening to resign in October of 1992. And you state that you were seeking to distance yourself and the party from all the negative conduct in Prijedor, and that your platform which you presented on the 5th of October, 1992, was the basic policy of the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, this 65 ter number was somehow transferred to 25720, so I think that's where you'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. Thank you very much. No, this is not what I'm looking for. If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, this is your 5th of October, 1992, proposal, is it not? Or platform, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, that's what I call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we can look at number 3, it says: "To publicly distance the party from any form of theft, misuse, and war profiteering, as well as any illegal and immoral activities..." And if we could quickly look at number 7, which should be on the next page, it says: "To return to our state all of the unlawfully appropriated material assets, machines, technical equipment, flats, money, et cetera, which are going to be necessary for its sustainment after the war." Now, of the ten points in this platform, these are the only two that address crime and the only crimes that are explicitly mentioned are theft and war profiteering. Now I take it that this reflects the fact that these were the crimes that you and others in the party were principally concerned with at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the platform it says, I think, since there were rumours which somebody probably spread deliberately, that behind all this dirty business in Prijedor, that is, all illegal business, there was the Serbian Democratic Party. Since this is not true, and since I was building my reputation, and I was known as a man of the law, and also to defend my own dignity and that of the party, I was forced to come forward with this platform, otherwise I would resign unconditionally. And I said that the board must adopt it, which was done. And this was the platform of the Prijedor Municipal Board at the time, and this was also our orientation. I mean political orientation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, you did not answer my question at all. My question was: Does the fact that the only two crimes mentioned explicitly in the document are theft and war profiteering reflect the fact that these were the crimes that you and the party were principally concerned with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it says, black on white, here: All illegal and immoral activities. That encompasses it all. So anything that was against the law, all sorts of crimes. It says in clear language. Nothing is left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you singled out theft and war profiteering. Doesn't that reflect your particular concern with these crimes, the fact that you singled them out in this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: You know how it was. These are the things that were most obvious to the people and you have to start with something; that is, looting, crime, and so on. You can't go item by item, though, and enumerate everything. And you must request all the authorities, including military authorities, to do their job in order to prevent such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back one page and look at number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this item of your platform discusses replacing company managers who supported other parties, Durakovic and Ante Markovic, with SDS personnel. And on the next page, still in item 4, the second-last paragraph of this item says: "This is the main reason why there is a certain degree of misunderstanding among some people in the Party, and among the Party" --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can barely hear you. Something is -- oh, no, now it's okay. Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It says -- this is still under 4: "This is the main reason why there is a certain degree of misunderstanding among some people in the Party, and among the Party representatives in the government." So it's clear from this document that the main cause of the conflict within the party in Prijedor was about personnel. It had nothing to do with crime at all; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: This is only one segment, just one bone of contention. The representatives of a party had entered a coalition with other parties, and I mean Ante Markovic's people from before the war and Durakovic's socialist party and the reformists. And it was our opinion that they had created or had given rise to all these negative things. And our representatives in the ruling structures had implemented all that through them. Of course, that was our view. We couldn't prove that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would tender this document, which is at pages 2 through 4 of this 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note my time is nearly up. This is my last topic and I think I can conclude it within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 1D25930. It now has an exhibit number. I am not sure what it is. It's an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, this is a document you discuss at paragraph 19 of your statement. It's your letter of the 19th of October, 1992, to Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacevic, and Mr. Drljaca, in which you ask these authorities to take action regarding illegal activities. And again, the only crimes that this letter explicitly identifies are looting, war profiteering, and abuse of office, and this is another reflection, is it not, of the fact that these were the crimes that principally concerned you and other party members at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: We were concerned by all crimes, but these crimes were all too obvious, because every house, every family gave their own contribution to the war, and this went on in front of their eyes. And of course they reacted. That's why we had to stress this. This is simply a request to the authorities to start activities to -- aimed at military and civilian structures to prevent all sorts of illegal behaviour. This is an additional appeal to all authorities, including the police, so that nobody could say that they weren't informed and that nothing -- that they weren't ask to do anything. Now, the army is a different thing. We didn't -- that was something else all together.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said, "These crimes were all too obvious," referring to looting, war profiteering, and abuse of office. Mr. Miskovic, the crimes like the massacre at Keraterm were obvious too, weren't they? Everybody in Prijedor knew about that. But you don't mention that much more serious crime in any of your letters and protestations and platforms, do you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent it was known, because it was kept secret. There may have been rumours. But nobody ever stated it officially. This was at an earlier time when the platform was adopted, and what you're referring to came later. And the platform, with its political statement, in fact, encompasses all sorts of illegal and immoral behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your platform is dated the 5th of October, 1992. The massacre at Keraterm had already happened; right? That was in July, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 16 of your statement, you - in discussing your 5th of October platform - you state that at the Municipal Board session the entire municipal leadership was dismissed for not having implemented this policy. Now just to be clear, Mr. Stakic and Mr. Kovacevic continued to serve as president of the municipality and president of the Executive Board until January of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: They are not party representatives. They are representatives of the authorities. And I -- and by this, Stakic, Kovacevic, Drljaca are meant. The ones we wanted replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They were all SDS members, weren't they? In fact, they were all Municipal Board members; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: They were SDS members, but not Municipal Board members. Drljaca was not, Stakic was vice-president, Mico Kovacevic was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all of them were members of the Municipal Board of the SDS. Milomir Stakic was a member and he was vice-president. He was also member of the Municipal Board. Mico Kovacevic, president of the Executive Board, was not member of the Municipal Board. Simo Drljaca was not a member of the Municipal Board. Who else was there? I forget. But they were not members of the Municipal Board. Stakic was a member and a vice-president, my vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stakic and Mr. Kovacevic continued to serve as president of the Municipal Assembly and president of the Executive Board until January 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Executive Board. I don't remember the date, but we launched activities to replace the people in leading positions, and there were problems. Soldiers with rifles came to our Assembly and there could have been a confrontation, but we tolerated them because we had nothing to hide. It was very cumbersome but we succeeded eventually. And the last one to be replaced was Simo Drljaca with the assistance of the party leadership. I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was in charge of that. But all previous attempts were unsuccessful. The minister of the interior, I believe his name was Hadzic, I am not sure, and he tried to replace him but without success.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, you talk in your statement and also at paragraph 16 about your efforts to have Simo Drljaca dismissed, which you state you managed to do with the assistance of Mr. Krajisnik, something you've just repeated.
