But, in fact, Mr. Drljaca was not exactly dismissed, was he? He was promoted and became assistant minister of the MUP, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that at that Assembly we were able to replace him because Krajisnik was there, and later on -- but later on, even Stakic returned. But at that period, we strove to replace these representatives of the authorities. There is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miskovic, at paragraph 17 you state that: "It is indisputable that SDS policy in Prijedor was not discriminatory towards any ethnic structure ..." The truth is, Mr. Miskovic, that the Prijedor municipal authorities, including Stakic, Drljaca, and Kovacevic, all of whom, as you've confirmed, were SDS members, were implementing the policy of the RS and SDS leadership to permanently remove non-Serbs from the municipality. That's why the crimes against non-Serbs continued for so long on such a massive scale. That's why no one from the municipal leadership was held accountable by the RS authorities for those crimes. That's why Mr. Drljaca was promoted. And that's why you and the municipal SDS leadership spoke out about crimes like looting and smuggling and ignored the far more serious crimes going on against Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: You can't really put it like that. I said, and the platform also reads, as far as our policy, our political position was that all crimes and all illegal activities, no matter who committed them, should be brought to justice. But we were not ones to do that. The hierarchy is known. The authorities, the police, and so on. It is clear who has power. The one who has weapons, especially at wartime. We cannot affect people's appointments or dismissals. You saw that we couldn't even prevent the army coming to our Assembly with long-barreled weapons. Perhaps we could have, but then there would have been a confrontation, and then what? So it was important to find the right measure and the right balance. That's what my platform says, too. It has to start at the top and then go down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I will not manage to conclude today. Are we going to work until 2.45 or 3.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can continue until 3.00, but -- if you like.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, but he must -- since he must come back tomorrow, you should decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a problem coming back tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Whatever you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miskovic, let's start with the last issues from the cross-examination as to how the Prosecution understands the power and role of the SDS. And let's connect this with the claim of the Prosecution, from page 75 of today's LiveNote, that on the 30th of April, 1992, the SDS took over power in Prijedor. Can you tell us whether the SDS indeed took over power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: From the documents, we see the term "take-over of power." However, we see from the documents that military structures, police structures were involved, in the effort to establish a Serb authority, a Serb government in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also accepted the contention that the take-over of power on 30th of April, 1992, was executed in keeping with Variant B. Can you tell us, according to Variant B, what does the Serb side take over, the whole municipality of Prijedor or the Serb municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was a leading -- that's a leading question. It just should have stopped with "what does the Serb side take over."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see, Your Excellencies, that it's not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you can simply ask what does the Serb side take over, as suggested by Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the Serb side supposed to take over, according to plan B? And what did it take over on 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: According to Variant B, in the event of threat to the Serbian people in that area, and to prevent that threat, the Serb side was supposed to take over power and that was done in the territories populated by a Serb majority. That's what I told Ms. Gustafson in her examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled Muslim parts of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: In all my previous statements I said and confirmed today, whenever we discussed this issue, that in the municipality of Prijedor, between Serb and Muslim areas there were check-points to prevent anyone who would want to create an incident in the other side's neighbourhood. And we succeeded in this effort. In this period there were no incidents in either Serb or Muslim neighbourhoods created by a member of the other ethnicity. In the same period, there were many talks and negotiations with prominent people, people who had authority from the other ethnic community, all with a view to preventing conflict, confrontation, and war. You can see all these various views expressed in talks, et cetera, but you have to understand that this area was severely victimised during the Second World War. We had to prevent all sorts of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak at a normal speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, Mr. Miskovic. You are speaking too fast, far too fast. You need to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you to caution me because I know I have this inclination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you need to repeat. So you repeat from: "We had to prevent all sorts of ..." If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to avoid confrontation we had to prevent anyone who would, for whatever reason, cause confrontation that would result in an avalanche, all in view of the experiences of that area from the Second World War, which you may not know about. It was a huge tragedy. Most of those who perished at the Jasenovac camp were children from Mount Kozara --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It's for Mr. Karadzic, but do you remember the question of Mr. Karadzic? What was his question now you're answering? So his question was: Who controlled Muslim parts of the municipality? Did you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did. They did. I answered that by talking about the check-points. In addition to that, we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- talks once or twice a day with some of their representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be brief. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please give us focused answers. You said that they controlled their own territories.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we controlled our own and there were check-points to prevent intruders going from one side to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until what time were these check-points tolerated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but I can tell you that the situation was peaceful, without a single incident on either side. All the way up to the moment when a Serb policeman by the name of Dzapa was killed. And the consequence of that, which was precisely what we feared and what we tried to prevent, is that his uncle intercepted a bus coming from Zagreb and killed several innocent Muslims, including by chance a colleague of my late wife, who was travelling from Croatia and had a Croatian ID. And there was -- and she was Serb, and she had trouble proving that she was Serb. Another incident was when soldiers were ambushed near Hambarine, when they were coming back from Slavonia. And a third incident was when a roadblock was placed on the road although we had agreed earlier that we would free up communications in the whole territory. That's when the road Prijedor-Banja Luka was blocked near Kozarac and Kozarusa. And as far as I know, the army came and intervened. Those are the three incidents that caused confrontation in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We shall not go into what happened during the Second World War, acknowledging the recommendation of the Honourable Presiding Judge, but please tell us, were there anymore recent reasons for your concern at the time? How did the other two sides behave?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as reasons for concern are concerned, and I stated that in my previous statements, was that we needed to divide powers after the multiparty elections. And later on, I concluded that the reason was that the Muslims had already entrenched positions. The president of the court -- [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really sorry. I tend to forget myself. This is what I do all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us who held which positions and how were the powers to be distributed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I explained it several times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take it easy and slowly. We are just wasting more time.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, check me when I start again. The misgivings were strengthened by the fact that the representatives of the SDA were evasive about this agreement on dividing powers because they already had entrenched positions. A Muslim was the president of the court, the public prosecutor, too, the chief of MUP, too, the commander of the station, too. Chief of Territorial Defence, Muslim; national defence, Muslims. So practically, apart from the JNA, the entire armed forces, both the reserve force and the police, were controlled be the Muslims. After the multiparty elections, there was supposed to be a levelling in the personnel, a more equitable ratio. So when I came to be the head of the party, I placed myself at the head of our delegation to avoid having information from secondary sources, and we started talks about the tax administration. And within two hours, we divided 50 per cent of all posts. That's what happens when everybody has good will. However, the next day the representatives of the SDA reneged on that agreement and stopped further talks. I suppose that's because the talks were leading to a more equatable ratio in the senior posts and this created misgivings among the Serbs. That's one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any organisation of paramilitaries in Prijedor, and how is this connected with the staffing in the so-called security ministries and et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no paramilitaries ever during the war in Prijedor. On the other hand, I was very surprised when I heard that an acquaintance of mine, Ecimovic, was the head of the Green Berets in Carakovo village. Why I was I surprised? Because I used to know him. He was a handsome man and we met each other in bars very often. He was rather fond of Bohemian life. And I asked Dr. Esad Sadikovic to go and talk to him and invite him to talk to me. I wanted to know what it's all about. And Esad Sadikovic really went. He went to Carakovo, and he came back and tells me -- can I say exactly in his words what he told me, as Esad told it to me or shall I modify it a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Choose your words yourself.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: He said: "This fool, he has taken the 84 gun, holding it between his knees, playing Rambo." I was shocked. However, through a combination of circumstances, this same Ecimovic, after the attack of Prijedor, which was captured, I met him in the barracks and I wanted to know why he was acting that way. And he -- all he said was: I know you, Miskovic. I suppose he was ashamed. And we had been together to Grace, to some workshop before, and I thought I knew him really well so I was really shocked by his new persona.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we are going to continue tomorrow, shall we adjourn here for the day. Mr. Miskovic, we continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I'd like to advise you -- I wanted to advise you to the not to discuss about your testimony with anybody else. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of December, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.57 p.m.,
